cf.title: [PATCH v1 0/1] Avoid carrying self lock-only xmax to updated tuple

input.subject: [PATCH v1 0/1] Avoid carrying self lock-only xmax to updated tuple

verdict_reasoning: Only standards-compat-1 survived, and it is a fixable level 2 point: after ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE the new row version shows xmax = 0 from SQL. No surviving objection questions the goal or the design. The open matter is whether the same-XID exception is correct under concurrency, and only a committer who knows heap tuple locking can sign that. Confidence is low because no code was read and no one in the visible thread reviewed correctness.

brief.title: Do not carry a self-owned lock-only xmax to the updated tuple
brief.problem: When a transaction locks a row and then updates it with the same XID, heap_update() copies its own lock-only xmax to the new tuple version. In patterns that repeat lock and update in a loop of subtransactions, later iterations then create, expand and reread MultiXacts. The author cites a 2019 thread that describes the same case for ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE and manual row locking.
brief.proposed_design: heap_update() treats an old xmax that is a single XID, lock-only, and equal to the updating XID as having no locker to carry, so the new tuple gets an invalid xmax. Remote lockers, a different subtransaction's lock, and MultiXacts keep the current behavior. v1 adds a README.tuplock section on the invariant; v2 drops the pageinspect test and updates the ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE expected output in update.out.
user_visible_surface: On-disk tuple state changes: in the same-XID case the new tuple version has xmax = 0 and HEAP_XMAX_INVALID, which pageinspect shows.
author_claims: A carried self-owned KEYSHR_LOCK | LOCK_ONLY marker has no concurrency or referential-integrity role, because the new tuple's xmin is the same XID.
In a repeated lock-and-update subtransaction loop with fsync off, 10000 iterations took about 126s before and about 27s after, about 4x faster.
The speedup applies to this repeated lock/update pattern only and is not a general UPDATE performance claim.
Remote key-share lockers, such as foreign key checks, stay protected.
brief.thread_state: João Rito tested v2 with make check and manual pageinspect checks, saw the expected tuple states, an unchanged foreign key case, and a similar speedup; he listed many untested areas. No one has reviewed the correctness of the same-XID exception, which the author asked for.
unclear: The material does not show whether v2 keeps the README.tuplock section.
No isolation test, check-world run, or concurrency stress test covers the change.
The proposal does not discuss effects on VACUUM, freezing, logical decoding, pg_upgrade, or replication of the new tuple state.
Lock modes other than FOR UPDATE taken first, such as FOR SHARE or FOR NO KEY UPDATE, are not tested.
The material does not say how the 2019 discussion ended or why that idea was not done then.
The entry is tagged Bugfix but targets version 20; the thread does not say whether a backpatch is intended.

objections.title: Updated rows from ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE now show xmax = 0
objections.failure_scenario: An application runs INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... RETURNING (xmax = 0) AS inserted, a widely copied idiom, to tell inserts from updates. After upgrade, every updated row returns inserted = true. The application miscounts or skips its update branch, and nobody notices until the data is wrong.
objections.argument: Message #5, test 3, shows that the patched server leaves xmax = 0 on the new version after ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, where it was the updating XID before. v2 changes the existing ON CONFLICT expected output in update.out, so the change is visible from SQL as well as through pageinspect. The idiom is undocumented, but a committer would likely want it named in the release notes, with a pointer to a supported way to tell inserts from updates. The Bugfix tag also suggests a backpatch, and making this change in a minor release would be harder to defend.
objections.author_must_show: Will the patch stay master-only with a release-note entry for applications that read xmax after ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, and what replacement will that entry point to?

critic.reasoning: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE locks the existing row and then updates it with the same XID, so today the new version carries that XID as xmax. Message #5 test 3 and the update.out change in v2 show it becomes 0, and the thread does not discuss the SQL-visible effect.

refuted.title: Same-XID exception may lose its README invariant and its focused test
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch to heap_update() or compute_new_xmax_infomask() changes how lockers are carried. It either brings back the self lock-only xmax or drops a remote locker in a nearby case. Only one update.out line covers the area, so the mistake ships unnoticed until a user hits a concurrency bug.
refuted.argument: The argument for safety rests on an invariant in tuple locking that few committers work on, and no one with that background has commented (message #5 tested only make check). v1 wrote the invariant into README.tuplock, but message #4 says only that v2 removes the pageinspect test, and the material does not show whether the README section survived. Without the README text and an isolation test, the special case lives only in a comment-free branch in heapam.c. A committer would likely ask for both before taking on this exception.
refuted.author_must_show: Does v2 keep the README.tuplock section, and which isolation test pins both the same-XID case and the remote and other-subtransaction lockers that must keep their xmax?

critic.reasoning: The scenario is an unnamed future patch that makes an unnamed mistake, which fits any change to heap_update(). The material shows no code, so "comment-free branch" has no support, and test coverage and README text are outside levels 1-2.

refuted.title: Bugfix tag suggests a backpatch of a tuple-locking behavior change
refuted.failure_scenario: The patch goes into back branches because it is tagged Bugfix. A minor release then changes the xmax that heap_update() writes, with only make check run on it. Any regression in locking or MultiXact handling shows up in production after a routine minor upgrade.
refuted.argument: The change fixes no wrong result: message #1 describes redundant MultiXact work and a performance gain for one loop pattern. Back branches normally do not take behavior changes in heapam locking for speed alone. The CommitFest entry targets version 20, but the Bugfix tag and the thread do not say whether a backpatch is intended.
refuted.author_must_show: Is this intended for master only, and if not, what wrong result in released branches would justify changing tuple-locking state in a minor release?

critic.reasoning: The CommitFest entry targets version 20 and no message asks for a backpatch. A CommitFest tag does not put a patch into back branches, because the committer decides that, so the scenario has no path to happen.

refuted.title: Benefit shown only for a synthetic subtransaction loop, no field report
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer changes how heap_update() sets xmax, which every UPDATE after a row lock in the same transaction goes through. The measured gain only covers PL/pgSQL loops that lock and update one row inside exception blocks. If that workload is rare in practice, a subtle visibility or freezing bug found later costs everyone, and only a few users ever benefited.
refuted.argument: The only numbers are the author's 10000-iteration loop with fsync off (message #1) and a single 3000-iteration debug-build run (message #5). No -general or -bugs report, production MultiXact story, or second user is cited. The 2019 link shows someone saw the redundant xmax, but the material does not say that anyone reported pain from it. For plain FOR UPDATE then UPDATE, or ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE without subtransactions, the proposal claims no measurable gain.
refuted.author_must_show: Which production workloads hit repeated MultiXact creation from self-locked rows in subtransaction loops, and how much MultiXact growth or latency do they see today?

critic.reasoning: The cost side is an unnamed "subtle visibility or freezing bug", with no concrete case. The patch adds no user-facing feature to maintain, and message #5 reproduced the speedup on the path the patch changes, in a loop that uses ordinary PL/pgSQL exception blocks.

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows heap tuple locking, MultiXacts and the xmax infomask rules in heapam.c would have to own it. No such person has reviewed the same-XID exception in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the correctness of the xmax that heap_update() writes after a same-XID row lock, with no time limit. A mistake here would be a concurrency or referential-integrity bug found in production.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v2 after v1 and asked for a correctness review, which suggests continued engagement.

priority.reason: The patch is small and adds no user-facing feature, and the measured gain covers lock-and-update loops in subtransactions. Review cost comes from the tuple-locking reasoning, and no one with that background has commented yet.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so this review cannot confirm that the exception excludes MultiXacts and other subtransactions as described, or that the old tuple's xmax handling is unchanged. No isolation or concurrency stress test covers the change.

precedents_retrieved.title: Make VACUUM remove MultiXacts with updater XIDs more eagerly
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes FreezeMultiXactId() so that VACUUM removes a MultiXact outright when all of its members are older than OldestXmin, instead of leaving it in place with FRM_NOOP processing. The goal is to get more use out of each GetMultiXactIdMembers() call and to remove more Multis that have updater XIDs, since OldestMxact can be held back much longer than OldestXmin.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The thread ends when Peter Geoghegan creates the CF entry. No message shows a reviewer objecting to this patch or the author explaining the withdrawal. Andres Freund's objections in the thread concern the separate patch that skips the TransactionIdDidCommit() sanity checks.

precedents_retrieved.title: Lock updated tuples in tuple_update() and tuple_delete()
precedents_retrieved.summary: When tuple_update() or tuple_delete() finds a concurrently updated tuple in read committed mode, the table AM locks the updated version itself instead of returning TM_Updated for a separate tuple_lock() call. Later versions also had update and delete return the old tuple through a slot passed by the executor, which avoids refetching it and helps table AMs with costly TID lookups.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Version 15 was committed in March 2023, then reverted after Andres Freund's post-commit review. He showed that RETURNING could use the wrong tuple, with an isolation test that fails. He also criticised the new API: the ignored wait parameter, tmfd turned into an input, and the LazyTupleTableSlot code. The redesigned old-tuple API came days before the version 16 feature freeze, and he said it was not ready for 16. In March 2024 the author planned to push a revised version, and the visible messages do not show why the entry was finally returned with feedback in October 2024.

precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I guess this really is part of my issue with this change - it optimizes the rare case, while not addressing the same inefficiency in the common case.

Earlier, Mark Dilger warned that a pattern no current code path creates may still have been written by a past release or upgrade path.

precedents_retrieved.title: Avoid computing ORDER BY junk columns unnecessarily
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a projection at the end of grouping_planner() that removes junk columns added only for ORDER BY or GROUP BY, so expensive sort expressions satisfied by an index are not computed. To mark which junk columns can be removed, it turns the resjunk boolean into an enum.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane found that the patch changes only the final top-level targetlist, so lower plan nodes still compute the expensive expression and cost estimates do not reflect the saving. He also thought the resjunk enum change was invasive and suggested waiting for the work on unifying index scans and index-only scans. Richard Guo found Assert failures with postgres_fdw and with FOR UPDATE queries, and CFbot later reported test failures with no new version posted.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: My basic complaint is that this is a band-aid that only touches things at a surface level, whereas I think we need a much deeper set of changes in order to have a plausible solution.

precedents_retrieved.title: Allow self-conflicting INSERT INTO .. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATEs
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE accept a command whose own proposed rows conflict with each other, as DO NOTHING already does. Today such a command fails with "command cannot affect row a second time".
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund and Peter Geoghegan voted against it, and the CFM returned it citing those two votes. Andres Freund objected that the patch makes one command update a row it inserted, producing cmin == cmax and breaking heap visibility rules. The author then found visibility bugs in his own patch. Peter Geoghegan argued that updating the same row twice in one command is not desirable and asked who would want it.

precedents_retrieved.title: CRC32C Parallel Computation Optimization on ARM
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch speeds up CRC32C on ARM with the 3-way parallel algorithm from an Intel whitepaper, using vmull_p64() carryless multiply to combine three block CRCs, with configure and meson checks for the crypto extension. John Naylor later reworked it to use a lookup table and software carryless multiply, which works on any input up to 8400 bytes and also on x86.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The whitepaper says its method derives from Intel patents, and the patent status of the technique stayed unclear. Bruce Momjian said that contributing code is a copyright matter, unrelated to patents, and that the community may have no way to accept patent usage grants. John Naylor returned the entry because the legal status was still unclear.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent matches. [P8] lets one INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE update its own inserted row twice, and [P1] changes how VACUUM freezes MultiXacts. Neither recorded reason applies to dropping a same-XID lock-only xmax in heap_update(). Message #1 cites a 2019 discussion of this case, but the material does not say how it ended.
There is no new syntax, GUC, catalog object or psql change, so there is nothing to check for pg_dump round-trip. The only user-facing effect is the xmax value seen from SQL.

The change creates no new persistent or cross-node state. The new tuple version gets xmax = 0 with HEAP_XMAX_INVALID, a state heap pages already hold everywhere, so no on-disk format, pg_upgrade, catalog, wire protocol or ABI change follows, and tuples already carrying a self lock-only xmax stay valid. The update WAL record already carries the new tuple's xmax and infomask from the primary, so a standby replays the primary's choice. A rolling upgrade or mixed-version standby sees no new record type. Logical decoding does not read the new version's xmax. VACUUM and freezing see fewer MultiXacts, not new states. The open question is whether the same-XID exception is correct against concurrent lockers, and that belongs to the locking-semantics angle. Without the code or isolation tests, this angle cannot confirm that the old tuple's xmax handling is unchanged.

The change has no privilege or exposure aspect. It only alters the xmax that heap_update() writes when the same XID locks and then updates a row; it adds no user, role or function, and exposes no new data. Whether it is correct under concurrency belongs to other angles.

From the maintenance and fit angle the idea belongs in core. It adds one comparison to heap_update() with no visible cost to users who do not use the pattern. It also makes an updated tuple look like a tuple freshly inserted by the same XID. The objections above concern how the change is kept safe and where it lands, not whether it is wanted.

No existing feature, extension or hook does this, because the change is inside heap_update() and how it fills in the new tuple's xmax. Rewriting the application avoids part of the cost, for example one UPDATE ... RETURNING in place of SELECT ... FOR UPDATE then UPDATE, but ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE takes its lock internally and users cannot avoid that.
Demand is the only concern from this angle. The change has no UI and the pattern is plausible, so this is a request to show demand, not grounds to reject.
